content: Diseases of poverty are illnesses that disproportionately affect individuals living in poverty compared to those who are wealthier. In many instances, poverty itself is the primary risk factor for these diseases. Conversely, certain diseases can also contribute to or exacerbate poverty. The three most significant diseases of poverty are AIDS, malaria, and tuberculosis. Developing nations bear the overwhelming burden of these illnesses, with 95% of global AIDS cases and 98% of active tuberculosis infections occurring in these regions. Additionally, 90% of malaria-related deaths are concentrated in sub-Saharan Africa. Collectively, these three diseases are responsible for 10% of all deaths worldwide. Other diseases closely linked to poverty include measles, pneumonia, and diarrheal diseases, which are often grouped with AIDS, malaria, and tuberculosis in discussions about diseases of poverty. Furthermore, infant and maternal mortality rates are significantly higher among impoverished populations. For instance, 98% of the 11,600 daily maternal and neonatal deaths occur in developing countries. Altogether, diseases of poverty claim the lives of approximately 14 million people each year. The mechanisms underlying the prevalence of these diseases among the poor are multifaceted. Malnutrition, along with inadequate or inaccessible healthcare, further impairs recovery and worsens the severity of these illnesses. Malnutrition is implicated in 54% of childhood deaths caused by diseases of poverty. Additionally, the lack of skilled healthcare professionals during childbirth is a major contributor to the elevated rates of maternal and infant mortality among impoverished populations. The consequences of diseases of poverty are profound and cyclical. These illnesses not only arise from poverty but also perpetuate it by draining both personal and national health and financial resources. For example, malaria has been shown to reduce GDP growth by as much as 1.3% in some developing countries. AIDS, which has claimed tens of millions of lives in sub-Saharan Africa, poses a severe threat to the economic stability, social structures, and political systems of entire societies. Malnutrition alone is responsible for the deaths of thousands of children every day. In some cases, diseases themselves are believed to contribute to poverty. This is particularly true for certain mental illnesses, which can impair social functioning, awareness, and cognitive abilities. Examples include autism, schizophrenia, antisocial personality disorder, and mental impairments caused by substance abuse or trauma. Malaria is also cited as a disease that can directly lead to poverty.
